title: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
summary: Defines STUN, a tool other protocols use to deal with NAT traversal. An endpoint can use it to learn the address and port a NAT gave it, check connectivity with another endpoint, and keep NAT bindings alive. On its own it is not a complete NAT traversal solution. It obsoletes RFC 3489 and was later replaced by RFC 8489.

plainLanguage.summary: Behind a mail room, you do not know your own outside address. STUN is like calling a friend outside who tells you what address they see on your letter.

questions: how to find your public ip and port behind nat
what is the stun magic cookie
how does stun find your public ip
subtitle: A small toolkit for learning your public address behind a NAT, meant to be used inside bigger NAT traversal solutions.

tldr.problem: Hosts behind a Network Address Translator do not know the public IP address and port the NAT gave them, and the original STUN of RFC 3489 tried to be a complete solution but did not work well enough to deploy.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a Binding request to a server on the public side. The server copies the request's source address and port into an XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS attribute in the response, so the client learns how it looks from outside.
tldr.outcome: STUN is redefined as a tool used by other NAT traversal solutions such as ICE. RFC 5389 obsoletes RFC 3489 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 8489.

today: RFC 5389 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8489, and it has also been updated by RFC 7350 and RFC 8553. It obsoleted RFC 3489, the classic STUN specification.

sections.title: What STUN Is and Why It Changed
sections.content:
Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) gives an endpoint a way to find the IP address and port that a NAT allocated for its private address and port. It can also keep a NAT binding alive. With extensions, it can run connectivity checks between two endpoints or relay packets between them.

STUN is not a NAT traversal solution by itself. It is meant to be used inside one or more solutions called STUN usages. A usage says when STUN messages are sent, which optional attributes are included, which server is used and which authentication mechanism applies. ICE and SIP Outbound are two usages named in the text.

The original STUN, now called classic STUN, in RFC 3489 presented itself as a complete solution: discover whether you are behind a NAT, classify its type, and learn your public address. Experience showed that it did not work well enough to be deployable. The address it found was sometimes usable with a peer and sometimes not, with no way to tell, and its NAT type classification was faulty because many NATs did not fit the defined types. It also had a security weakness that no cryptography could fix. For these reasons RFC 5389 obsoletes RFC 3489, and renames the protocol from Simple Traversal of UDP through NAT to Session Traversal Utilities for NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: The first version of STUN tried to do the whole job of getting past the mail room and often got it wrong. This version just does one small, reliable job and lets other tools do the rest.

sections.title: How a Binding Transaction Works
sections.content:
STUN is a client-server protocol with two kinds of transactions. In a request/response transaction the client sends a request and the server answers. In an indication transaction either side sends a message that gets no response. Both carry a 96-bit transaction ID that is randomly chosen.

This RFC defines one method, Binding. When a Binding request crosses a NAT, the NAT rewrites its source address and port, so the server sees the public address created by the NAT closest to it. The server copies that source address into an XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS attribute in the Binding response. The NAT will change the destination address of the response packet, but not the address inside the attribute, so the client learns its reflexive transport address. Binding indications are used to keep NAT bindings alive, and simply receiving one refreshes the bindings in the NATs along the path.

Over UDP, reliability comes from the client retransmitting the request, starting with an interval called RTO and doubling it each time. The default is to send up to 7 requests in total. With an RTO of 500 ms, requests go out at 0, 500, 1500, 3500, 7500, 15500 and 31500 ms, and the transaction is considered failed if no response arrives by 39500 ms. Indications are not retransmitted. Over TCP and TLS-over-TCP, TCP handles reliability, and the client treats a request as timed out after Ti seconds, which defaults to 39.5 s. UDP messages should stay below the path MTU; for IPv4 with an unknown path MTU that means a STUN message under 548 bytes.

A Binding request is idempotent, so a server can answer a retransmitted request by recomputing the response instead of storing state for each transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: You shout your name across a big yard and a friend on the other side shouts back where your voice seemed to come from. If you hear nothing, you shout again, a little later each time.

sections.title: The STUN Message Format
sections.content:
Every STUN message starts with a 20-byte header followed by zero or more attributes. The header holds a message type, a message length, a magic cookie and the transaction ID. The two most significant bits are always zero, which helps tell STUN packets from other protocols that share the same port.

The 14-bit message type packs a 12-bit method and a 2-bit class. Class 0b00 is a request, 0b01 an indication, 0b10 a success response and 0b11 an error response. A Binding request is encoded as 0x0001 and a Binding success response as 0x0101. The magic cookie is always 0x2112A442. It was carved out of the 128-bit transaction ID of RFC 3489, which is why the transaction ID is now 96 bits. The message length counts the bytes after the 20-byte header, and because every attribute is padded to a multiple of 4 bytes, its last two bits are always zero.

Each attribute is encoded as type, length and value (TLV), with a 16-bit type and a 16-bit length, padded to a 32-bit boundary. Types from 0x0000 to 0x7FFF are comprehension-required: an agent that does not understand one cannot process the message. Types from 0x8000 to 0xFFFF are comprehension-optional and can be ignored. Key attributes include:

  • XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS: the reflexive address. The port is XORed with the top 16 bits of the magic cookie, and an IPv4 address with the cookie. An IPv6 address is XORed with the cookie plus the transaction ID. This is done because some NATs rewrite any 32-bit value that looks like their public address.
  • MAPPED-ADDRESS: the same address in plain form, used by servers only to stay compatible with RFC 3489 clients.
  • SOFTWARE: a diagnostic description of the sender's software.
  • ERROR-CODE and UNKNOWN-ATTRIBUTES: carry failures. See the error codes below.
sections.plainLanguage: Each STUN message is a form with a fixed top part and then optional extra boxes. The top says what kind of message it is and carries a special stamp, so anyone can quickly tell it is really STUN.

sections.title: Authentication and Optional Mechanisms
sections.content:
STUN defines optional mechanisms that each usage may choose. Two are for authentication and message integrity, both based on an HMAC-SHA1 stored in the MESSAGE-INTEGRITY attribute (20 bytes).

  • Short-term credentials: client and server first agree on a username and password by some other means, for example the signaling used by ICE. Each request carries USERNAME and MESSAGE-INTEGRITY, and the password is never sent. The HMAC key is the password after SASLprep.
  • Long-term credentials: a provisioned username and password, with a digest challenge. The client first sends a request with no credentials. The server rejects it with a 401 error that carries a REALM and a NONCE. The client retries with its username, the realm and the nonce, plus an HMAC. The key is the MD5 hash of username:realm:password. If the nonce expires, the server answers with a 438 (Stale Nonce) error and a fresh nonce. This mechanism cannot protect indications, because they cannot be challenged.

Other optional mechanisms:

  • FINGERPRINT: a CRC-32 of the message XORed with 0x5354554e, always the last attribute, which helps recognize STUN when it is multiplexed with other protocols.
  • DNS discovery: clients look up SRV records with service name stun, or stuns for TLS. If there are none, they fall back to A or AAAA records. The default port is 3478 for TCP and UDP and 5349 for STUN over TLS.
  • ALTERNATE-SERVER: a server can redirect a client with a 300 (Try Alternate) error. The error must be protected by message integrity, and a client must ignore a redirect to a server it already tried within the last five minutes.

A basic stand-alone STUN server only has to support the Binding method over UDP and TCP, and it should not use authentication, because authenticating a request costs more than answering it.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the friend answering your call should check that it is really you. You can agree on a secret phrase ahead of time, or the friend can hand you a one-time word to repeat back.

sections.title: Error Codes and Receiving Rules
sections.content:
A receiver first checks that a message follows the rules: the first two bits are zero, the magic cookie is right, the length is sensible and the method and class are valid. Messages that fail these checks are silently discarded. Unknown comprehension-optional attributes are ignored. A request containing unknown comprehension-required attributes gets a 420 error with an UNKNOWN-ATTRIBUTES attribute listing them.

Error responses use the ERROR-CODE attribute, whose codes follow SIP and HTTP. Clients treat 300 to 399 as failure unless ALTERNATE-SERVER is in use, treat 400 to 499 as failure, and may resend after a 500 to 599 error, but must limit how often they do so.
sections.plainLanguage: If a message looks wrong, a STUN agent just ignores it. If it is a real request the agent cannot understand, it sends back a short note saying what went wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who can modify packets on the path can break STUN, but message integrity detects this. An attacker who only observes traffic, for example on Wi-Fi, could race in a fake error response, which integrity protects against except for authentication-related errors. Running STUN over TLS removes these attacks. Because the integrity key comes from a shared secret, offline dictionary attacks are possible, so strong passwords are needed.

The more serious problem is a faked reflexive address. An on-path attacker can alter the source address of a Binding request, and message integrity cannot prevent this, since NATs must be able to change that address. The text describes four attacks built on this: a distributed denial of service against a target, silencing a client, assuming the identity of a client and eavesdropping. Its suggested remedy is for the client to verify the address it learns, as ICE does. The RFC also describes a plan to move to a new hash if HMAC-SHA1 is ever compromised, and recommends making the SOFTWARE attribute configurable since it may reveal vulnerable versions.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person in the middle could trick you about where your letters come from. So the clever part is double-checking the address you were told before you rely on it.
